units.translation: For seven men, impetuous leaders of companies.
And seven lordly rulers of the host.
They were twice a hundred and seven.
And the seven daughters of Atlas, named.
Seven against Thebes
having seven gates
having seven gates
the seven-gated seat of the city (I added "of the city") (i.e. Thebes) of the flowing river
seven-flowing
seven-flowing. Of the Nile having seven mouths.

Thus I corrected what is read in the manuscript: ἐνθάδε Νεῖλος ἑπτάρρους [here the seven-flowing Nile], which was ignorantly changed by others to ἔνθα Νεῖλος ἑπτάρους [where the seven-flowing Nile]. Similarly χειμάρροον [winter-flowing] is placed at the end of a trimeter in fr. 280.
From the land of Ethiopia, where the seven-flowing Nile rolls the earth with the rain of winds.
here the seven-flowing Nile

winter-flowing

Sept. 284 εἰς ἑπτατειχεῖς ἐξόδους [to the seven-walled exits], i.e. the seven exits of the walls.
i.e. the seven exits of the walls.

incantation
incantation
My father did not make incantations for these.
enchanter
enchanter. Of one who averts evil.
where it is used in the feminine gender, which Hesychius and Suidas noted: ἐπῳδός [enchantress]: she who sings incantations over the sick.
He sacrificed his own child, an enchanter of Thracian winds.
enchantress: she who sings incantations over the sick
to sit on eggs, to brood
I sit on eggs, I warm the eggs by sitting on them.

Aeschylus in Niobe (fr. 158) metaphorically: ἐφημένη τάφον τέκνοις ἔπωζε τοῖς τεθνηκόσιν [sitting on the tomb she brooded over her dead children]. "The grammarian is foolish; for neither Aeschylus nor any other poet could ever compare a mother fixed to the tomb of her children to a hen sitting on eggs. One should read ἐπῷζε [she lamented]. The verb ἐποίζω [I lament] is easily supported by the cognate δυσοίζω [I lament greatly]." NAUCK. on Arist. Byz. p. 162.
to sit on eggs: to sit upon the eggs.
Aeschylus in Niobe
metaphorically sitting on the tomb she brooded over her dead children
she lamented
I lament
I lament greatly
surname, name
surname, name
of Eteocles and Polynices.
Rightly according to their names they perished, and much-quarreling.
And by the name the fated life was fulfilled, rightly.
named after, eponymous
named after, eponymous. It is said of one who has received a name from something, and is joined with either the genitive or the dative.
said of Ocean, i.e. Oceanus.
leaving the eponymous stream
And the Bosporus will be called by that name.
And you will bear the eponymous offspring of Zeus, dark Epaphus, by touching (thus Wieseler for "offspring").
Of whom Zeus the averter may be called by name for the city of the Cadmeans.
the city named after Cadmus
To him who bears this overweening sign, it would rightly and justly be a name.
not a mind named after maidens
And very much by name, I mean Polynices.
My mother, having acquired a mind not named after her children, god-hated.
And know that you are very much named after the escort.
I know the race and the eponymous omens.
And they sacrificed to Ares, whence the rock and the hill of Ares are named.
And of my lord, rightly named, the race of the Pelasgians.
Epaphus truly named from the deliverance.
to oversee, to watch over
I inspect.
i.e. he governs.
How many things you oversee, and things well placed out of the way.
